name: Canva AI-assisted coding interviews
citation: Primary: Simon Newton, 'Yes, You Can Use AI in Our Interviews. In fact, we insist' (subtitle: 'How We Redesigned Technical Interviews for the AI Era'), Canva Engineering Blog, 11 June 2025, https://www.canva.dev/blog/engineering/yes-you-can-use-ai-in-our-interviews/. Companion: Karl Hörnlund, 'AI Interview Success: An Interviewer's Inside Guide' (subtitle: 'From the Other Side of the Screen: What We're Looking For in Your AI-Assisted Interview'), Canva Engineering Blog, 20 October 2025, https://www.canva.dev/blog/engineering/ai-interview-success/. Note: the companion post is by Karl Hörnlund, not Simon Newton.
evidence_tier: Primary company statement (both are posts on Canva's own engineering blog). The companion post is a single interviewer's practitioner perspective published on the company blog.
access_status: Fully read. Both pages were fetched in full (HTML retrieved and stripped to text) on 2026-11-21.
sponsor_and_incentive: Canva itself. Both posts end with a recruiting call to action ('Check out our current openings and experience our AI-assisted interview process for yourself'), and the first ties the change to Canva's 'AI Everywhere' philosophy, so there is an employer-branding and recruitment incentive to present the change positively. No external funding; Canva does not sell AI coding tools, though it builds AI features into its own product.
exact_quotes: Newton, para 1: "we now expect Backend, Machine Learning and Frontend engineering candidates to use AI tools like Copilot, Cursor, and Claude during our technical interviews."
Newton, 'The Reality of Modern Engineering': "At Canva, almost half of our frontend and backend engineers are daily active users of an AI assisted coding tool."

Newton, same section: "Our interview approach included a Computer Science Fundamentals interview which focused on algorithms and data structures. This interview format pre-dated the rise of AI tools, and candidates were asked to write the code themselves."

Newton, 'Our Philosophy: Transparency Over Detection': "Rather than fighting this reality and trying to police AI usage (which is increasingly difficult!), we made the decision to embrace transparency and work with this new reality."

Newton, same section: "Our initial experiments confirmed what we suspected: AI assistants can trivially solve traditional coding interview questions. When we tested our Computer Science Fundamentals questions with AI tools, they produced correct, well-documented solutions in seconds, often without requiring any follow-up prompts or clarification."

Newton, same section: "With AI tools generating initial code, a critical skill is the ability to read, understand, and improve that code. Our traditional interviews gave us no signal about these essential capabilities."

Newton, 'Embracing Complexity and Ambiguity': "we redesigned our questions to be more complex, ambiguous, and realistic - the kind of challenges that require genuine engineering judgment even with AI assistance. These problems can't be solved with a single prompt"

Newton, same section: "instead of asking a candidate to implement Conway's Game of Life, we might instead present them with a challenge like: \"Build a control system for managing aircraft takeoffs and landings at a busy airport.\""

Newton, 'Introducing AI-Assisted Coding Interviews': "We've piloted a new competency we called \"AI-Assisted Coding\" that replaces our traditional Computer Science Fundamentals screening for backend and frontend engineering roles."

Newton, same section (evaluation criteria): "Do they understand when and how to leverage AI effectively? How well do they break down complex, ambiguous requirements? Can they make sound technical decisions while using AI as a productivity multiplier? Can they identify and fix issues in AI-generated code? Can they ensure AI-generated solutions meet production standards?"
Newton, 'Addressing Internal Concerns': "The initial reaction was worry that we were simply replacing rigorous computer science fundamentals with what one engineer called \"vibe-coding sessions.\""
Newton, same section: "We're still assessing computer science fundamentals through the new process, and we expect engineers to take full ownership of any code they produce"

Newton, 'What We've Learned': "The most successful candidates didn't just prompt AI and accept whatever it generated." They "Asked thoughtful clarifying questions about product requirements", "Used AI strategically for well-defined subtasks while maintaining control of the overall solution", "Critically reviewed and improved AI-generated code", "Demonstrated strong debugging skills when AI solutions had issues".

Newton, same section: "candidates with minimal AI experience often struggled, not because they couldn't code, but because they lacked the judgment to guide AI effectively or identify when its suggestions were suboptimal."

Newton, 'Looking Forward': "The early results are promising. Our AI-assisted interviews feel more engaging for both candidates and interviewers, and they're providing strong predictive signals about candidate performance."
Newton, 'Looking Forward': "What works today may need refinement in six months as AI capabilities advance and new tools emerge."
Hörnlund, opening: "I've had the pleasure of conducting many AI-assisted programming interviews since we launched this new format."
Hörnlund: "We want to see you use AI like the productive engineer you'll be on day one."
Hörnlund, 'Development Phase': "Throughout, they maintain production-quality standards, ensuring the code could be submitted as a pull request for peer review."

Hörnlund, 'Common approaches that don't shine': "AI Showcase" ("we're more interested in seeing strong engineering fundamentals amplified by AI tools"), "Feature Marathon" ("We'd rather see thoughtful problem-solving and quality code than a rushed feature list"), "Hands-Off" ("treating it as a complete solution generator rather than a development accelerator").

Hörnlund, 'What we're actually evaluating': three areas, "Engineering Problem-Solving", "Technical Depth & Ownership" ("Do you understand and own the code in your solution?"), and "AI Collaboration Effectiveness" ("Can you critically evaluate AI outputs and iterate toward better solutions?").
Hörnlund, 'During the interview': "If your interviewer asks you a question, tell us what you think before getting help from AI"
Hörnlund, 'Summary': "We're assessing your engineering capabilities enhanced by AI collaboration, not your AI skills in isolation."
date_and_recency: Newton post published 11 June 2025; Hörnlund post 20 October 2025. No data-collection window, pilot dates or candidate counts are given. Tools named are Copilot, Cursor and Claude, with no model versions. The claim that AI 'trivially' solves the old CS Fundamentals questions refers to tools available in or before mid-2025. Newton himself flags that the approach 'may need refinement in six months'.
key_claims: 1) Canva now expects Backend, Machine Learning and Frontend engineering candidates to use AI tools (Copilot, Cursor, Claude) in technical interviews. 2) The old Computer Science Fundamentals interview (algorithms and data structures, written without AI) did not evaluate how candidates would perform in the actual role. 3) Policing covert AI use is increasingly hard, so Canva chose transparency over detection. 4) Canva's own tests found AI tools solved its CS Fundamentals questions correctly in seconds, often without follow-up prompts. 5) Engineering work is mostly reading, reviewing and improving code; the old interview gave no signal on that. 6) Questions were redesigned to be more complex, ambiguous and realistic (e.g. an airport takeoff/landing control system instead of Conway's Game of Life) so they cannot be solved with a single prompt. 7) A piloted 'AI-Assisted Coding' competency replaces the CS Fundamentals screening for backend and frontend roles. 8) CS fundamentals and code fluency are still assessed, just in a different context, and candidates must own all code they produce. 9) Successful pilot candidates clarified requirements, used AI for well-defined subtasks while keeping control, reviewed and improved AI output and debugged; candidates with little AI experience struggled for lack of judgment in guiding AI, not inability to code. 10) Early results are 'promising', more engaging, with 'strong predictive signals'. Companion post (Hörnlund): the strongest interviews look like an experienced engineer building a real feature, across planning, development and discussion phases; weak patterns are 'AI Showcase', 'Feature Marathon' and 'Hands-Off'; interviewers assess engineering problem-solving, technical depth and ownership, and AI collaboration effectiveness; candidates should give their own view before asking the AI and should be able to discuss trade-offs, improvements and scaling at the end.
headline_figures: Only one number in either post: "almost half of our frontend and backend engineers are daily active users of an AI assisted coding tool" (Canva internal engineers, frontend and backend only, as of June 2025; no denominator or measurement method given). Also qualitative timing: AI produced correct CS Fundamentals solutions "in seconds". Newton anticipates refinement "in six months". No candidate counts, pass rates, interviewer agreement, or performance-correlation figures are reported.
sample_and_method: Software engineers. No formal study. Evidence is (a) an internal informal test of Canva's CS Fundamentals questions against AI tools, (b) an unspecified pilot of the new interview with an unstated number of backend and frontend candidates, and (c) one interviewer's accumulated experience of 'many' interviews (Hörnlund). Findings are qualitative interviewer impressions; no method for the 'predictive signals' claim is described.
what_is_measured: Engineering judgment while directing AI on a realistic, ambiguous product problem: decomposing ambiguous requirements and asking clarifying questions; deciding when and how to use AI; making sound technical (design and scope) decisions; reading, reviewing, debugging and fixing AI-generated code; holding output to production standards and owning the code; explaining and defending decisions and trade-offs afterwards (communication). Canva says CS fundamentals and code fluency are still assessed within this context. Explicitly not measured in isolation: AI tool skill or prompting tricks (the 'AI Showcase' anti-pattern) or raw feature throughput ('Feature Marathon').
ai_policy_in_interview: Required. Candidates are expected to use their preferred AI tools and are told in advance; Canva recommends practising beforehand.
scope_and_status: Piloted, then launched. Newton (June 2025) says the 'AI-Assisted Coding' competency was piloted and replaces the CS Fundamentals screening for backend and frontend roles; the opening sentence also includes Machine Learning candidates in the AI-use expectation. Hörnlund (October 2025) says 'since we launched this new format' and that he has run many such interviews, implying it is in regular use. Whether it is company-wide across all engineering levels, and how it fits other rounds, is not stated. [uncertain]
validity_evidence: None published. Newton asserts the interviews provide 'strong predictive signals about candidate performance' but gives no criterion data, no correlation, no sample size, no follow-up of hires, and no comparison with the old CS Fundamentals interview. Treat as an unsubstantiated company claim.
relevance_to_angle: Strong support for 'stop testing convergent coding': Canva dropped its algorithms/data structures round explicitly because AI solves those questions in seconds, and replaced Game of Life style puzzles with open-ended product problems. Supports 'working with an agent': AI use is mandatory and the assessment centres on guiding, reviewing and correcting AI output. Supports 'design conversation': the planning phase (scope, assumptions, architecture sketch) and the closing discussion of trade-offs, improvements and scaling are explicitly assessed. Supports 'communication': think aloud, explain and justify every decision, give your own view before consulting AI. Supports 'basic fluency' in two senses: candidates must set up an AI-integrated environment and project in advance, and Canva still says code fluency and CS fundamentals are required. Complicates the angle slightly: Canva frames this as a re-contextualised fundamentals test rather than abandoning fundamentals, and team fit is not addressed in either post.
limitations_stated: Newton acknowledges internal concern that the change replaced rigour with "vibe-coding sessions" (he says it was resolved by explaining fundamentals are still assessed). He acknowledges candidates must adapt: "We're mindful that this shift requires candidates to adapt." He flags shelf life: "What works today may need refinement in six months as AI capabilities advance and new tools emerge." Hörnlund's post states no limitations. Neither post acknowledges the absence of quantitative evidence.
counter_evidence: No data supports the 'strong predictive signals' claim; it is self-reported by the employer in a recruiting post. The finding that candidates with minimal AI experience struggled may mean the format partly measures prior tool familiarity, which could disadvantage strong engineers new to AI tools and reward a skill that is quick to learn. Interviewer judgments of 'AI collaboration effectiveness' and 'judgment' are subjective and no rubric, calibration or inter-rater data is published. Allowing candidates to bring their own tool and pre-built project setup adds uncontrolled variance between candidates. The 'almost half' daily-use figure means a large share of Canva's own engineers were not daily AI users at the time, which slightly undercuts the 'reflects the job' rationale. Internal engineers' initial 'vibe-coding' objection is a documented critique, answered only by assertion.
verification_status: All claims, quotes and figures above were checked against both primary posts, opened in full on canva.dev on 2026-11-21: verified. Exception: the scope beyond backend/frontend (whether ML roles go through the same replacement round, and whether rollout is company-wide) is ambiguous in the source itself and marked [uncertain]. Secondary coverage (The Register, Information Age) describes Newton as Canva's head of platforms; his job title does not appear in the post and was not verified. [uncertain]
